$comment: What kit's shell owner (text/shell.cjs) reads as a write, as data, so no command or language is a case in code; a command's name is read without its folder, an @version and its version digits. cd: commands that move the working folder (popd and a cd to no named folder lose it). skip: shell words before the command itself. shells: a shell and the option (a regular expression) whose next word is a command string, or whose `code` group is that string (trap's first word); a heredoc or here-string fed to it is one too. evals: commands that run their words as a command. redirects: the operators that write a file. devices: a target that holds nothing, so it is no file written (`-` is the standard stream). commands: one row per command. Its options are read the getopt way: `--name=value` is that option with its argument; a word a row field names whole is one option (find -delete); else each letter of `-abc` is an option `-a`, `-b`, `-c`, and the first that takes an argument holds the rest of the word, or the next word where nothing is left. Every field is a regular expression over one option (`-e`, `--expression`) or one word, unless said: takes, an option with an argument of its own, never an operand; glued, an option whose argument, if any, is only the rest of its word (sed -i.bak); out, an option whose argument is a file written (curl -o), or an operand whose `path` group is one (dd of=); chdir, an option whose argument is a cd for this command alone (git -C); into, an option whose argument is the folder its operands land in, all of them sources (cp -t); sub, the row of the subcommand its first operand names; runs, the words after one matching it up to one matching until, or (a number n) from its operand n on, are a command it runs (a row that runs a command or has a sub reads no option of its own after its first operand); item, a word there that is a file it hands that command, and items (true), one more such word at the end; when and unless: its operands are written where a when option is given, or no unless option is (either alone decides); whole, an option that makes it write files its text does not show (git reset --hard, git checkout -f, find -delete); bundle (true), an old-style first word without a dash is a bundle of options (tar xzf); script, an option that gives the script (`^$`: none does), else its first operand is the script, no file (a mode, an owner, flags), but only where every long option is one the row names (getopt_long takes an abbreviation); maybe (true), its first operand before `--` names a commit or a file, a file only where the caller finds one there (git checkout main, git checkout app/x.rb); writes, which operands it writes: all (bare true: none named is the folder it runs in, `.`), last (its sources named, so a folder destination can be placed), move (all, the last with its sources) or unplaced (it writes files its text does not show). code: inline code, read by text/shell-code: option, the option whose next word is code for any command that is no shell or runner, or whose `code` group is code glued to it (-e'...'); a heredoc or here-string fed to a command that writes nothing itself is code too; no interpreter is named, whatever runs it, its write calls are read. calls: one write call each, a `path` group the file it writes, which may hold one call of its own (`os.path.join(...)`, unplaced, never unseen), none where its text cannot be read; in every pattern no two runs of spaces touch (each optional token owns its spaces) and no unbounded part runs past the next start of the same pattern, so a long or hostile line is read in linear time; assign: an assignment, `name` (a sigil kept), `op` (none or `:` sets) and the `value` up to the line's end, a `;`, a `}` or an `=` (then it cannot be read); heads: a function head, its `name` and `params`; param: one parameter's name; loops: a loop, block or tuple assignment that binds its `names` (`,` or `=>` between) to what the text does not show; text and comment: what code does not run (text/shell-blocks skips them: triple quotes, a regex literal, `#` to the line's end, `//` on its own line, `/* */`), so a brace or a `;` there opens, ends or stops nothing; start: what may stand between a statement's start and the name it sets (a declaration word), for an assignment that begins its statement; plain (an allow-list): a statement read in full, its literals one operand and its comments nothing: unread, a character outside the few it may hold (a quote left open, a `%` literal, a `\`) or a heredoc `<<`; outside its brackets, operands joined by operators (an assignment, a call, a chain), a name given literals only (a command), one of ends alone, or anything that ends in a block it saw open and close; control, words that are never a name or a call there (they head a body or skip one); opwords, words that join or lead operands; loads, words that, first, load a module (the rest is names, literals and lists); any other statement (an unknown word, a name beside a name, an operator last) may hide a body, so no assignment after it in its block surely runs;literal, name and join: a path expression, string literals and names joined; interpolates: a literal's text a language expands, which no one can place.
